header.title: 🔬 Reflection and refraction simulator
header.subtitle: Explore how light behaves at the boundary between two media

lawReflection.title: Law of reflection
lawReflection.explain: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

lawSnell.title: Snell’s law (refraction)
lawSnell.explain: Relates the angles and refractive indices in the two media.

critical.title: Critical angle
critical.explain: Minimum angle for total internal reflection (when n₁ > n₂).

rainbow.title: Rainbows
rainbow.body: Rainbows form from refraction and reflection of sunlight in atmospheric water droplets. Each colour has a slightly different refractive index, which produces spectral separation.

diamond.title: Diamond sparkle
diamond.body: Diamond has one of the highest refractive indices (n = 2.42), giving frequent total internal reflection and its characteristic brilliance.

fiber.title: Optical fibre
fiber.body: Optical fibres use total internal reflection to guide light over long distances with little loss. Modern internet relies heavily on this technology.

pool.title: Pools look shallower
pool.body: When you look into water, objects appear closer to the surface than they really are, due to refraction as light passes from water to air.

mirage.title: Mirages
mirage.body: Desert mirages come from refraction in air layers at different temperatures. Hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index.

glasses.title: Spectacle lenses
glasses.body: Glasses correct vision using refraction: converging lenses (for hyperopia) and diverging lenses (for myopia) steer light to focus correctly on the retina.

tech.indexBody: Refractive index (n) is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed in a given medium. The larger n, the slower light travels in that medium.
tech.tirBody: When light goes from a denser medium (larger n) to a less dense one and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, all light is reflected back into the first medium.
tech.dispersionBody: Refractive index varies slightly with wavelength. Blue light (smaller λ) refracts more than red (larger λ). This is called dispersion.

tips.text: Feather vs hammer — In air the feather drifts slowly because drag is huge. In vacuum (slider at 0) both fall IDENTICALLY — as on the Apollo 15 Moon demo.
Flat vs crumpled paper — Same mass, different shape! The flat sheet has much larger area, so air slows it enormously. Crumpled falls almost like a ball.
Tennis vs bowling ball — Similar spheres but very different mass. The bowling ball hits the ground much sooner in air, though in vacuum they would fall together.
Coin vs feather — Dramatic in air! The coin slices through with tiny area while the feather is braked heavily. Compare terminal speeds!
Basketball vs steel ball — The basketball is heavier but its huge area yields a surprisingly low terminal speed. The steel ball falls much faster.
Brick vs feather — Extreme contrast! The brick is barely affected by air (~48 m/s terminal speed) while the feather floats near ~3 m/s.

header.title: Quantum tunnelling
header.tagline: The electron is not a classical particle — it is a probability wave.

theoryLeft.title: Probability wave, not a trajectory
theoryLeft.p1a: In quantum mechanics, the electron is not a ball with well-defined position and speed before measurement. It is described by a
theoryLeft.p1b: \(\psi(x,t)\), a complex quantity that evolves according to the Schrödinger equation.
theoryLeft.p2a: Born’s rule: the probability of finding the particle between \(a\) and \(b\) is \(P(a \le x \le b) = \int_a^b |\psi(x,t)|^2 \, dx\).
theoryLeft.p2b: is \(\rho(x,t) = |\psi|^2\). In the simulation, the violet “mist” shows \(|\psi|^2\) (discretely normalised on the grid).
theoryLeft.p3b: localises \(\psi\) in space and propagates as a group; the width \(\Delta x\) and momentum \(\Delta p\) obey (in order of magnitude) \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \gtrsim \hbar/2\).
theoryLeft.p4c: slider sets the energy associated with the packet in the demo scale;
theoryLeft.p4d: controls the height \(V\). The ratio \(E/V\) decides whether tunnelling or “going over” dominates.

theoryRight.title: Tunnelling, reflection and transmission
theoryRight.p1a: , if \(E \lt V\), a particle with energy \(E\) would not pass over the barrier.
theoryRight.p1b: , in the region \(V(x) > E\) the solution has an
theoryRight.p2b: the barrier and, after width \(a\), can emerge beyond it with transmission probability \(T\) (tunnelling). For \(E > V\) inside the barrier, the wave is oscillatory (\(\sim e^{\pm i k' x}\)); at interfaces there is
theoryRight.p3b: of height \(V_0\) and width \(a\), with \(E \lt V_0\), transmission decreases roughly exponentially with \(\kappa a\): \(T \sim e^{-2\kappa a}\) (order of magnitude; prefactors depend on details). In the simulation, \(R\) and \(T\) are simplified analytical models.
theoryRight.caption: for \(E \gt V_0\) (rectangular barrier).
theoryRight.note: The visualisation is educational; exact coefficients follow from matching \(\psi\) and \(\mathrm{d}\psi/\mathrm{d}x\) at the barrier edges.

mathAria.rectangular: Rectangular barrier with E greater than V₀

modes.below: The electron tunnels through the barrier: the wave enters the classically forbidden region and a reduced amplitude appears beyond it.
modes.above: The electron passes classically over the barrier (energy above the potential); reflection and transmission oscillate with barrier width.
modes.equal: At the limit E = V, between tunnelling and propagation over the barrier, the coefficients depend sensitively on geometry.

info.intro: This simulator shows the double-slit experiment in the quantum regime. Particles (electrons or photons) do not have an exact position; they are described by a wavefunction that gives the probability of detection.
info.waveP: The wave is not “matter”, but information about where the particle might appear. Brighter regions mean higher probability.
info.interferenceP: When the wave passes through two slits it interferes with itself. That produces high- and low-probability fringes.
info.detectorP: When the detector is on, we learn which slit was used. That destroys interference and the pattern becomes classical: two simple bands.
info.colorsP: The heat map shows probability (ψ²): red = high probability, blue = low.
info.whyP: This phenomenon is central to quantum physics and underpins electrons in atoms, chemical bonding, and much of modern technology.
info.try1: Turn the detector off → see interference
info.try2: Turn the detector on → fringes disappear
info.try4: Increase slit separation → fringes move closer together

page.eyebrow: Heavy water (D₂O vs H₂O) | Interactive simulation

hook.a: What happens if you drink heavy water?
hook.b: Can water shut down a nuclear reactor?
hook.tease: H₂O and D₂O share the same chemical skeleton, but different nuclear masses: deuterium (²H) is almost twice as heavy as protium (¹H). That is why differences show up in biology (isotope exchange), in reactors (neutron capture) and in spectra (vibration frequencies). Pick a mode below.

bonus.p1: Dorel Mihai Constantinescu (b. 1947, Râmnicu Vâlcea) is the Romanian physicist associated with the period when Romania developed its own heavy-water facilities. In the 1970s, at the G plant in Râmnicu Vâlcea, he led the computing laboratory that modelled isotope separation processes and helped obtain the first quantities of D₂O in experimental flow. He also worked on design linked to the complex at Drobeta-Turnu Severin, an important node in the national heavy-water chain.
bonus.p2: In 1976 he was recognised as inventor for a deuterium separation plant using isotope exchange; in 1977 he received a PhD in physics, and in 1981 the Romanian Academy awarded him the Dragomir Hurmuzescu prize. He published on the history of technology in Râmnicu Vâlcea, documenting the experience of a generation of specialists in the nuclear field.

body.desc1: In organisms, water acts as a solvent and as a hydrogen source in enzymatic reactions. D₂O has properties similar to H₂O, but O–D bonds are “heavier” than O–H: some reaction rates drop (kinetic isotope effect), and very high D₂O fractions cause serious physiological effects. In natural water, deuterium is present at about 140 ppm (roughly 0.014% of hydrogen atoms, i.e. about one D per ~7000 H).
body.desc2: The slider sets a fictitious molar fraction of D₂O in a model liquid; the cell grid is for visual intuition only, not a diagnosis.
body.disclaimer2: Educational demo. Do not drink heavy water.

story.vlow: Very low value, close to the natural deuterium background in water (~140 ppm). In the model, the visual effect is essentially zero.
story.low: Low fraction: almost all molecules are still H₂O; in reality, organisms tolerate trace D₂O without obvious effects.
story.mid: Moderate fraction: in the model, the D₂O share increases; in animal experiments, moderate D₂O fractions affect rates of some hydrogen-dependent reactions.
story.high: High fraction: real toxicity rises with dose; in humans, large body fractions of D₂O are dangerous
story.vhigh: Very high fraction: an extreme scenario for on-screen demonstration only.
story.max: 100%: the maximum in the model. In reality, massive D₂O exposure is not something to test — it is harmful.

reactor.desc1: Fission releases very energetic (“fast”) neutrons. To use them efficiently in fuel rods, they must be slowed to thermal energies — called moderation. Molecules around the fuel (heavy or light water) collide with neutrons and reduce their energy.
reactor.fact1: CANDU reactors (e.g. Cernavodă): D₂O moderator, often natural uranium fuel.
reactor.fact2: With H₂O, capture on hydrogen is higher; many designs use enriched fuel instead.
reactor.hintD2o: D₂O: small capture cross section on deuterium; neutrons lose energy via elastic collisions and remain available for fission in the fuel (simplified model).
reactor.hintH2o: H₂O: hydrogen absorbs thermal neutrons in the moderator; fewer neutrons reach the fuel — many light-water reactors use enriched uranium.
reactor.fateD2o: D₂O moderator: small neutron losses in the water; in CANDU design, the chain can be sustained with natural uranium (~0.7% ²³⁵U).
reactor.fateH2o: H₂O moderator: larger losses on hydrogen; in this model the chain thins — in practice this is compensated with enriched fuel or other measures.

physics.panelTitle: H₂O and D₂O: same geometry, different mass
physics.intro: The water molecule has an H–O–H angle of about 104.5°. Replacing ¹H with ²H increases molecular mass by over 10%, while geometry stays similar. Infrared and Raman spectra show lower vibration frequencies for D₂O; as a liquid, D₂O is denser and boils slightly above 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
physics.abundP: Natural deuterium: ~140 ppm (~0.014%) of hydrogen; ordinary water contains only traces of D₂O.
physics.radioP: Ordinary D₂O is not radioactive; tritium (³H) is a different isotope, present only in traces.
physics.thermoP: At standard pressure, D₂O boils near ~101.4 °C — slightly above H₂O — because of bonding and higher mass (hydrogen-bond picture).
physics.massExpP: For a simple harmonic oscillator, a mode frequency depends on reduced mass μ: f ∝ 1 / √μ. In D₂O, μ is larger than in H₂O for similar motions, so characteristic frequencies are lower. The slider tweaks a simplified μ ratio between D₂O and H₂O.
physics.densityP: At the same temperature, one litre of D₂O weighs ~11% more than one litre of H₂O — relevant to isotope separation and industry.
physics.quizQ1: 1. At 1 atm, which boils at the higher temperature?
physics.quizQ2: 2. In CANDU design with natural uranium, the typical moderator is:
physics.quiz1ok: At atmospheric pressure, D₂O boils near ~101.4 °C, slightly above H₂O (100 °C), because of bonding and mass.
physics.quiz1bad: D₂O has a higher boiling point than H₂O at the same pressure.
physics.quiz2ok: Natural-uranium CANDU reactors use a D₂O moderator to limit neutron losses.
physics.quiz2bad: Hydrogen capture in H₂O is high; classic CANDU does not use light-water moderator with natural uranium.

header.title: Full simulation of the Michelson–Morley experiment
header.desc: Explore the interferometer, rotation, fringes and the (hypothetical) ether effect. Adjust every physical parameter to see how the interference pattern changes.

theory.title: Theory and calculations — Michelson–Morley
theory.p1: The interferometer compares travel times along two perpendicular arms. In the classical ether picture, the time difference between arms after a 90° rotation is about Δt ≈ 2 L v² / c³, and the maximum fringe shift on rotation is ΔN ≈ 2 L v² / (λ c²). The phase is Δφ = 2π ΔN.
theory.note: Historically the result was null (no fringe shift was seen), which helped lead to special relativity.

hero.title: Fission simulator
hero.subtitle: Watch how a single neutron starts a chain reaction in uranium-235.

info.title: How it works
info.p1: A slow neutron hits a U-235 nucleus, forming unstable U-236. The nucleus splits into smaller fragments and releases 2–3 new neutrons, plus about 200 MeV of energy.
info.p2: If fuel density exceeds critical mass, the reaction becomes self-sustaining and the k factor rises above 1.
info.tip: Click anywhere on the reactor to launch a neutron.
